slides.name: BRIEF ANATOMY AND PHYSIOLOGY OF THE HEART AND AN INTRODUCTION TO ECG COMPILED AND PRESENTED BY AO IDRIS Learning Objectives •By the end of this session, participants should be able to: •Describe the basic structure of the heart. •Identify the main chambers, valves, and layers of the heart. •Understand the cardiac conduction system and how it generates electrical impulses. •Understand the basis of ECG. Pre-presentation MCQs 1. What is the primary function of the heart? A) To filter blood B) To generate nerve impulses C) To pump blood throughout the body D) To produce red blood cells 2. Which of the following chambers pumps oxygenated blood into systemic circulation? A) Right atrium B) Right ventricle C) Left atrium D) Left ventricle 3. What is the name of the valve between the left atrium and left ventricle? A) Tricuspid valve B) Pulmonary valve C) Aortic valve D) Mitral (bicuspid) valve 4. Which of the following is NOT a typical indication for performing an ECG? A) Chest pain B) Syncope C) Sore throat D) Palpitations 5. What is an electrocardiograph? A) The process of performing an ECG B) The graphical output of heart activity C) The machine used to record the ECG D) The heartbeat itself Overview of the Heart •The heart is a muscular organ about the size of a fist, located in the thoracic cavity. •It functions as a double pump to circulate blood throughout the body. •Divided into four chambers: •Right Atrium (RA) •Right Ventricle (RV) •Left Atrium (LA) •Left Ventricle (LV) •Separated by valves that control blood flow and prevent backflow. Circulation Pathways •Right heart (pulmonary circulation): •RA receives deoxygenated blood from the body → RV pumps it to the lungs via the pulmonary artery. •Left heart (systemic circulation): •LA receives oxygenated blood from the lungs → LV pumps it to the rest of the body via the aorta. •This closed-loop system ensures tissues receive oxygenated blood and waste is removed. Heart Valves and Their Role •Four valves ensure one-way flow: •Tricuspid valve (RA → RV) •Pulmonary valve (RV → pulmonary artery) •Mitral valve (LA → LV) •Aortic valve (LV → aorta) •These open and close in response to pressure changes in the chambers. Layers of the Heart Wall •Endocardium –Inner lining of the heart chambers. •Myocardium –Thick muscular layer responsible for contraction. •Epicardium –Outer surface of the heart. •Pericardium –A protective double- layered sac encasing the heart. •ECG measures electrical activity in the myocardium, so understanding this layer is essential. Function Histology of the Heart •The cardiac tissue are divided into conductive tissue and contractile tissue in the myocardium. •The conductive (nodal) tissue comprises special modified nerve cells that initiate and conduct rhythmic depolarisationsof the myocardial cells. •Nodal cells: SA Node, intermodal pathways, AV node, AV bundle (Bundle of His), Bundle branches (left and right). •Contractile cells: Actin, Myosin, Tropomyosin, Sarcoplasmic reticulum The Cardiac Conduction System •The heart has an intrinsic electrical system to generate and propagate impulses. •Key components: •SA node (Sinoatrial node): naturalpacemaker, initiates heartbeat. •Internodalpathways: i.Bachmannsbundle ii.Wencheback iii.Thorel •AV node (Atrioventricular node): delays impulse to allow atrial contraction. •Bundle of His: transmits impulse to ventricles. •Right and Left Bundle Branches: conduct down each ventricle. •Purkinje fibers: spread impulse throughout ventricles. Action Potential in nodal cell Action potential in contractile cell Electrical Activity and Cardiac Cycle •The heart undergoes: •Depolarization –electrical activation → muscle contraction. •Repolarization –return to resting state → muscle relaxation. •Systole = Contraction, Diastole = Relaxation •These phases are reflected in the ECG waveform. Cardiac Cycle Cardiac Cycle Introduction to ECG: Brief History •1849:EmilduBois-Reymondfirstdiscovers electricalactivityinanimalhearts. •1887:AugustusWallerrecordsthefirst humanheartsignalusingacapillary electrometer. •1903:WillemEinthoveninventsthefirst practicalelectrocardiograph(usesthestring galvanometer). •HeintroducestheP,Q,R,S,Twave nomenclaturestillusedtoday. •AwardedNobelPrizein Physiology/Medicinein1924. •ModernECGsaredigital,portable,and essentialindiagnostics. Introduction to ECG •Electrocardiography: The process of recording the heart's electrical activity using an ECG machine. •Electrocardiograph: The instrument/device used to record the ECG. It amplifies and displays electrical signals from the heart. •Electrocardiogram: The actual recording or tracing produced by the electrocardiograph. Indications for ECG Diagnostic Purposes: Chest pain (to rule out myocardial infarction) I.Palpitations or irregular heartbeat II.Syncope (fainting) or dizziness III.Shortness of breath or unexplained fatigue IV.Suspected electrolyte imbalances (e.g., hyperkalemia) V.Preoperative assessment in patients with cardiovascular risk. •Monitoring Purposes: I.Ongoing cardiac conditions (e.g., arrhythmias, ischemia) II.Response to medications (e.g., antiarrhythmics, digoxin, QT-prolonging drugs) III.Pacemaker function IV.Post-MI or post-surgical follow-up Contraindications and Limitations There are no absolute contraindications to performing a standard 12-lead ECG. However, caution is needed in the following cases: •Skin infections or burns at electrode sites •Severe trauma or fractures (e.g., rib fractures that make lead placement painful) Limitations of ECG: •May appear normal in early or small infarctions •Not reliable for detecting mechanical problems (e.g., valve disease, heart failure) — needs echo •Interference from movement, tremors, or loose electrodes can distort tracings •Does not measure cardiac output or pump function •Silent arrhythmias may be missed in a single snapshot Common diagnosis made with ECG 1. Arrhythmias •Atrial fibrillation •Atrial flutter •Ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation •Bradycardia, Tachycardia, AV blocks 2. Myocardial Ischemia or Infarction ST-elevation MI (STEMI) Non-ST elevation MI (NSTEMI) Old infarcts (Q waves) 3. Electrolyte ImbalancesHyperkalemia(peaked T waves) Hypokalemia(U waves, flat T) Calcium abnormalities (QT changes) 4. Conduction Abnormalities Bundle branch blocks (LBBB/RBBB) AV blocks (1st, 2nd, 3rd degree) 5. Drug Effects or Toxicity Digoxin effect QT prolongation from medications Clinical Relevance •Understanding cardiac anatomy and physiology is critical for: •Correct ECG lead placement. •Identifying abnormal rhythms (e.g., atrial fibrillation, heart block). •Recognizing ischemia or infarction patterns (e.g., ST elevation). •A solid foundation here aids accurate interpretation and diagnosis. Summary •The heart is a four-chambered pump with a unidirectional flow system. •Electrical impulses arise from specialized cells and travel in a predictable pattern. •The ECG records these electrical events, which reflect underlying anatomy and physiology. •Basic knowledge of the heart’s structure helps make sense of complex ECGs. Q&A Which part of the conduction system delays the impulse to allow ventricular filling? A) SA Node B) AV Node C) Purkinje Fibers D) Left Bundle Branch References / Further Resources •Books: •"Rapid Interpretation of EKGs" by Dale Dubin •"Anatomy & Physiology Made Incredibly Easy" •Websites: •www.ecglibrary.com •www.teachmeanatomy.info •https://smart.servier.com
